en: Preface to the *Jiake Zhao Lun* (The Zhao Treatise with Interlinear Commentary),
composed by the Śramaṇa Huída of Xiaozhaotí Monastery,
annotated by Chan Master Lètán Xiàyuè.
△ An outline of this introductory section is divided into two chapters. The first clarifies the original cause for composing the treatise; this is the general introduction (*sāmānyanidāna*).

The second correctly clarifies the fundamental tenets of the treatise; this is the specific introduction (*viśeṣanidāna*). Within the first part, which clarifies the original cause for composing the treatise, there are six sections:

First, the designation of the title of the treatise; Second, the praise of the person and the Dharma; Third, the expression of joy at having encountered [the teaching]; Fourth, the rejection of criticism and suspicion.
Five, restating the original circumstances; six, elucidating the intent of the preface. Now, first, the title of the treatise is set forth:

"Huida, leading his own ignorance, has compiled this general preface composed by the Dharma Master Śramaṇa Sengzhao of Chang’an, concerning the four treatises beginning with ‘The Fundamental Principle:
Things Do Not Shift’."

The master of the preface says, "Leading the ignorant. This is a phrase of humility and self-effacement. Regarding the term "preface" (*xu*), the *Erya* states: "The eastern and western walls are called the *xu*. Guo Pu’s commentary notes:
"It is for the purpose of ordering and distinguishing the interior from the exterior. Now, Master Da’s preface recounts the original causes for composing this treatise;

it is like the eastern and western walls serving as the preface to a residence. Furthermore, the preface is like a cocoon— [Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the extant portion.]

He obtained the prefaces (*xu*). The prefaces exhausted the silk of a single cocoon; the scriptures and commentaries obtained their prefaces, and the prefaces exhausted the principles and meanings of those scriptures and commentaries.
Regarding what is called Xiaozhaotiche Monastery: it is located in Jiangning County of Runzhou. It was formerly Danyang Commandery.
Beginning from the Wu dynasty and continuing through the six dynasties of Jin, Song, Qi, Liang, and Chen, the Buddha-dharma flourished there. As for the monasteries...
The Blue Vihāra adjoins Jianlian, their roof ridges meeting and their names paired together. For instance, Zhuangyan Temple has both a Great Zhuangyan and a Small Zhuangyan;
Zhaoti Temple likewise has the designations of "Great" and "Small," with the Great Zhaoti having been constructed during the Liang dynasty.
The Xiao-Zhaoti Temple was built during the Jin dynasty. Master Da was a person of the Chen period; he resided at Xiao-Zhaoti Temple as a śramaṇa.
Since there were many individuals named Da during the Chen era, his temple name is specified here for the sake of distinction.
Nevertheless, this Master Da’s understanding of Buddhist doctrine was not yet refined, and the literary style of the treatises and prefaces he composed often contained vulgar expressions.
Now, I shall simply set forth the general purport of this introductory discourse; may later readers refrain from derision. The *Zhao lun* (Treatise by Sengzhao) is named after its author.
He was a native of Chang’an during the Later Qin dynasty under Emperor Yao Xing. His secular surname was Zhang. Being poor, he made his living as a copyist of books;
through his skill in transcription, he eventually came to examine the classics and histories exhaustively, mastering the entirety of the ancient records. Then...
As a Confucian scholar, he deeply savored the profound and subtle mysteries, constantly taking the teachings of Zhuangzi and Laozi as his essential core.
He would often read the "Daode Chapter" of Laozi and sigh, saying: "Beautiful indeed it is; yet its methods for dwelling the spirit and transcending worldly burdens are still not exhaustive.
Later, upon encountering the ancient *Vimalakīrti Sūtra*, he examined and relished it, whereupon he remarked: "Only now do I know where to turn. Thereby...
This renunciant, Daotong Shixiang, was barely in his early twenties when his brilliant eloquence became widely renowned.
Later, when Kumārajīva came from the East to convert and guide others, he stayed briefly at Guzang. Sengzhao hurried there to pay his respects and followed Kumārajīva to receive instruction.

Whatever writings he had previously composed, he presented them all to Kumārajīva, who leaned on his desk and sighed in admiration, saying: "That which I have created is profound and subtle; I need not feel ashamed before you."
His literary style was elegant and beautiful; in substance, he followed the truth and could be ranked among those of virtuous fortune. He subsequently accompanied Kumārajīva to Chang’an.
Yao Xing ordered Sengzhao, along with Sengrui and others, to reside in the Xiaoyao Garden to meticulously determine and finalize the sutras and śāstras.
He composed the *Zongbenyi*, *Wubhiquan*, *Buzhenkong*, the three treatises on "Prajñā has no knowledge," and the *Niepan wuming lun*.

These were written only after Kumārajīva had passed away. Upon seeing these treatises, Liu Yimin of Mount Lu sighed and said, "I did not expect that among those in the saffron robes there would again be a 'Ping-shu' (a scholar like Wang Bi). He presented them to Master Huiyuan, who—

He then leaned upon his desk and sighed, saying, "Never before has there been such a thing. Thereupon, he began to examine and savor its meaning, and subsequently composed the *Wuming lun* (Treatise on Namelessness) and sent it to Master Zhu Fashih for inquiry.
After Master Kumārajīva passed away, he further composed three chapters of the *Baocang lun* (Treasury of Jewels).

He presented [the work] to the Prince of Qin, Yao Xing. The Prince responded with great courtesy and issued an edict to have it transcribed and distributed among his sons and nephews as a great instruction.
Such was the esteem in which he was held by his contemporaries.
In the tenth year of the Yixi era of the Jin dynasty, he passed away at the Xiaoyao Garden in Chang’an at the age of thirty-one. △ Second, the section on "Beautiful Women."
The propagation of the Dharma in the final age belongs truly to the Bodhisattvas of the Four Reliances; that it has been transmitted to this land is likewise an instance of this principle.
As for the "final age," it refers to the period after the Buddha’s parinirvāṇa when the True Dharma declined, during which time masters such as Aśvaghoṣa appeared in India to compose [treatises].
In interpreting the sutras and extensively protecting the Buddha-dharma, those who are truly worthy are those who can be relied upon with faith. There are two kinds of "Four Reliances":

first, reliance on persons; second, reliance on the Dharma. Regarding reliance on persons: Bodhisattvas prior to the stages of the ten abodes, ten practices, and ten dedications are called *srotāpanna* (Stream-enterers) and constitute the first reliance.
Bodhisattvas of the first stage (*bhūmi*) who have attained the path of vision are called *sakṛdāgāmin* (Once-returners) and constitute the second... [reliance].
The second reliance: Bodhisattvas from the stage of entering the second bhūmi up to the eighth bhūmi on the path of cultivation are called *anāgāmins*;
this constitutes the third reliance. Bodhisattvas from the eighth bhūmi up to the full realization of the tenth bhūmi are called *arhats*;
this constitutes the fourth reliance. Regarding the two reliances upon the Dharma: first, rely on the meaning and not on the letter; second, rely on wisdom and not on consciousness. Third...
Rely on the Dharma, not on the person; rely on the definitive meaning, not on the non-definitive meaning.
As for "transmitted to this land," it refers to when the teachings reached this territory. Furthermore, as for "those such as," it refers to the various patriarchs of India and so forth.

As for the great virtuous monk Kumārajīva, whose reputation filled the heavens, he and his fellow monastics were all pioneers who established the fundamental tenets, delineated the principles of knowledge, and propagated the teachings.
What they pursued was the profound and the void; this alone constitutes the ancestral source of the sage-like silence.

The "Great Virtuous One who Encompasses Heaven" was the Dharma Master Dao’an of Xiangyang. This originated from the discourse on the "Discourse on Emptiness" (Kongxue lun) by the Regional Inspector Xi Zuochi.
One day, Master Xi visited Dao’an and said, "Xi Zuochi of the Four Seas has come specifically to pay my respects."
It happened that they were meeting for the first time; Dao’an replied at once, "The monk Shi Dao’an under the vast sky (Miti) shall see you after the meal.
From this time on, people called him the Great Virtuous One of the Vast Sky (Miti Dade). As for Kumārajīva (Tongshou), his name was also Luoshì. He was originally a native of Kucha;
his father’s name was Jūmārayāna and his mother’s name was Jīvā. She was the daughter of the King of that country.
"Pure Sister," combining the names of both parents, he is called Kumārajīva. Translated into the language of China (Huayan), this means "Child-Life" (Tóngshòu).
As for "Shi," it is because the Dharma Master Da delighted in the literary style and phrasing of this region; thus, the Chinese and Indian terms are combined as "Róushí.
Master Dao'an composed the *Treatise on the Emptiness of Nature*, while Master Kumārajīva composed the *Treatise on the True Mark*. In this land...
Regarding the beginning of the composition of these treatises: the term "sengmen" (桑門) is not the correct transcription of the Sanskrit sound;

it should be "shamen" (沙門). Translated into Chinese, it means "diligent cessation. This refers to those who have left the household life: seeing what is good, they diligently cultivate it; seeing what is evil, they cease from it.
These two masters both took the wondrous nature’s perfect luminosity as the fundamental principle (*mūla*) and composed these two treatises, intending to provide a comprehensive exposition.

Their distinct systems of measurement and principles were widely disseminated and proclaimed; their expositions and narratives all converged upon the essence and meaning of Prajñāpāramitā, and thus they are called "profound and empty" (xuánxū).
Master Dá praised these two individuals for composing their treatises, noting that they were the first to initiate a profound resonance with the Buddha’s principles.
Therefore, it is said that this alone is the model for the Sage’s silence, which is its source. First, to drum forth the principles of the Dharma is to model oneself after the Sage;
second, to maintain the Sage’s silence is to follow its source. It is both illumination and constant stillness, and stillness and constant illumination.
This preface praises both masters, Dao'an and Kumārajīva.

From the time they appeared until the present, throughout all successive eras, ancient and modern, this includes those monks whose names are recorded in the various monastic biographies (*sengzhuan*), as well as those not contained therein.
There were over three thousand monks, including Shi Sengrui and others, and approximately eight hundred lay devotees, including Xie Lingyun and others.

They were able to discern and rectify regional dialects, refine the structure of the text, thoroughly investigate the teachings of names and principles, and meticulously search for the underlying meanings;
they thus took the lead in the discourse of this assembly of worthies.
The phrase "down to oneself" (*jiǎng hū yǐ huán*) is not the standard literary form; it should rather be "down to this [point] and oneself" (*jiǎng sī yǐ huán*).

Throughout the successive generations of antiquity and the present, this has been the established practice for the prefaces of masters and their commentaries since the time of Dao’an and Kumārajīva. Regarding "throughout antiquity," this refers to the Later Qin in Chang’an to the northwest.
Regarding "throughout the present," this refers to the Western Jin, Eastern Jin, and Liang dynasties in the Jiangnan region. In all cases...
Throughout antiquity and the present, scholars have jointly translated Buddhist scriptures and composed treatises based upon them. Among the monastics, Master Rui was the first to lead the way;
among the laity, Lord Xie was the foremost. Thus it is said that they "bowed to this assembly of worthies.

While they were able to use words and phrases to skillfully embellish the Buddha’s intent, none of them attained the Middle Way; they merely unified principle and phenomena within the realm of language.
There is a man of such beauty who transcends both speech and silence. In establishing the fundamental principles, every sentence deeply penetrates the Buddha’s mind;
in clarifying the secondary details, every word fully comprehends the various teachings. Truly, this is a magnificent scripture of the Mahāyāna and a vast treatise of the Vaipulya.

This preface’s author praises Master Sengzhao for composing the Four Treatises (*Sishilun*), which profoundly accord with the ultimate and conventional truths and the principles and phenomena. Their nature and characteristics are quiescent and illuminating;
their essence and function are both transcendent. They do not lean toward either side of dependence. When it says, "There is one who can be praised as such," it refers to Master Sengzhao.
As the *Mao Shi* says: "There is a beautiful person, radiant and graceful; meeting by chance, it fulfills my wish.
And as the *Lun Yu* says: "What a gentlemanly person he is! Now, these two phrases from the two texts are combined into a single sentence.

Regarding the statement that [Daosheng’s work] "transcends speech and encompasses silence," this means that while the two masters preceding him, Kumārajīva and Sengrui, attained the principle (*li*), they were deficient in literary expression;

whereas Master Sengrui and Lord Xie produced treatises that attained the literary expression but were deficient in the principle. Now, Daorong’s Four Treatises (*Si Lun*) are complete in both principle and literary expression;

therefore, it is said to be "transcendent. This does not mean that his principle and literary expression surpass those of the four individuals mentioned before. This is the meaning of the term "standard" (*biao*).
"Fundamental" (ben) refers to the primary meaning of the school's tenet. "Clarifying the derivative" (mingmo) refers to the *Nirvāṇa-śāstra*. "Truly it is" (liangshi):

"truly" (liang) is glossed as "to believe. To believe that these four treatises on the meanings are no different from the *Avataṃsaka*, the *Śūraṅgama*, and other Mahāyāna teachings is to profoundly penetrate the Buddha-mind.

From antiquity to the present day, those who have composed writings and essays have meticulously examined and refined the various treatises produced by renowned sages— whether the six schools and seven sects,
or the twelve traditions of Yuan Yan— judging their merits and demerits and discerning their respective strengths and weaknesses.
This clarifies the strengths and weaknesses of the treatises composed by various masters. "Zhi Faxiang" refers to Zhi Faxiang, a disciple of Zhi Dun who took his teacher’s surname.

"Tai" refers to Zhu Fatai, a disciple of Zhu Daoyou. Zhi Faxiang composed the *Shixiang lun* (Treatise on the Reality-Characteristic), while Zhu Fatai composed the *Benwu lun* (Treatise on Original Non-being);
both possess their own merits and flaws. Regarding these two individuals, they are recorded in the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks).
They succeeded one another as renowned sages. Regarding the six schools and seven tenets: "yuan" (爰) signifies slowness; "duan" (短) signifies brevity; "yan" (延) signifies length.
Within these twelve treatises, there is much debate over right and wrong, long and short, good and evil. "Zang" (臧) means good; "fei" (否) means evil.
These various distinctions, though precise, all fail to accord with the Middle Way within the Buddha’s mind. — Liang Shi.

Baoshang compiled the *Sūfǎ lùn* (Treatise on Secular Laws) in one hundred and sixty fascicles. Within it, he cites the eminent monk Tánjì of Song Zāngyán Temple’s *Liùjiā qīzōng lùn* (Treatise on the Six Schools and Seven Tenets).
This treatise identifies six schools, which are further divided into seven tenets. The first is the School of Original Non-existence (*běnwú zōng*).
The second is the School of Original Non-existence of Profound Mystery (*běnwú xuánmào zōng*), which emerged from the first School of Original Non-existence. The third is... [text continues]
The School of Form (Se-zong). The Fourth is the School of the Conjunction of Meanings (He-zong), also called the School of the Conjunction of Consciousness (Shi-he-zong).

The Fifth is the School of Illusory Transformation (Huan-hua-zong), also called the School of Like an Illusion (Ru-huan-zong). The Sixth is the School of the Non-existence of Mind (Xin-wu-zong). The Seventh is the School of the Assembly of Conditions (Yuan-hui-zong), also called the School of Realizing the Essence (Ti-hui-zong).
Originally there were six houses; the first house was divided into two schools, thus forming seven schools. As for the mention of "twelve," it refers to the continuation [of the lineage].
The *Fǎlùn* (Discourse on the Dharma) states: "Below [this], Shi Huìjìng of Dinglin Monastery composed the *Shíxiàng liùzōng lùn* (Treatise on the Six Schools of the True Mark).

First, he established a hypothetical question regarding the principle that the two truths are of one essence, and subsequently answered it by citing the doctrines of the six schools. The first school takes ultimate reality as emptiness;
ordinary people perceive existence as being, such that emptiness is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and existence is the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*). Second..."
The first school holds that the emptiness of the nature (*dharmatā*) of form is emptiness, while the substance of form is existent as a conditioned phenomenon (*saṃskṛta*).
The third school holds that the absence of a mountain apart from its conditions is emptiness, while the mountain formed by causes and conditions is existent.

The fourth school holds that the mind arising from conditions is emptiness, while a distinct mind-substance apart from conditions is existent. The fifth school holds that the mind as conceived by false views is [emptiness].
Emptiness is emptiness; that which is not empty—the mind produced by causes and conditions—is existence.
The sixth school holds that the substance upon which name-and-form (nāmarūpa) depends is truly empty, while that which is conventionally designated within worldly usage is existence.
There are six schools in the former group and six schools in the latter, making twelve in total; hence it is said, "Yuan Yan’s twelve [schools]. As for "praise and censure":
The first six schools judge the fourth [position] to be erroneous, while the remaining five schools judge it to be correct.
In the subsequent six schools' treatises, they debate that among the first five schools, the former [four] are mistaken and the latter [fifth] is correct.
Only this treatise is free from such faults.
"Constitution" (xian) refers to the Dharma. Among the twelve previous schools, all possessed the faults of being either right or wrong;
however, the four treatises of Master Daosheng are now free of these faults, being entirely correct and devoid of error.
This is truly because his inner disposition is as vast and expansive as the sky, such that one knows not to what it is bound. He is like the deep ocean, whose volume exceeds the nine currents;
he rises loftily in pure emptiness, dwelling in serene detachment beyond the realm of mundane things.

"Generally speaking, 'by many' means that it is frequent. The preface praises Master Zhao’s spirit and the field of his emotions as being vast and expansive, like a deep abyss or a sea that has no boundaries or limits;
hence it says, 'it is likened to that abyssal sea. The character 'pi' (譬) is used here in the sense of 'likeness' or 'analogy.

Regarding the phrase 'its numbers surpassing the nine currents,' this praises Master Zhao’s literary style as being like the sea, transcending all numerical measures. The 'nine' refers to the Nine Schools."
There are two types of schools: first, those based on persons; second, those based on subjects. Regarding those based on persons, this refers to conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

The learning of Confucius was like the ocean, while the various masters and hundred schools were divided into nine streams: first, the Confucian stream; second, the Daoist stream; third, the Mohist stream;
fourth, the Logician stream; fifth, the Eclectic stream; sixth, the Agrarian stream; and seventh, the Diplomat stream.
The Nine Schools (*jiǔliú*). The second [point], regarding the naming of the nine schools based on their objects of study, also refers to them as the "Nine Rivers" (*jiǔjiāng*).
These are the great floods of the world that Yu the Great dredged and diverted, dividing them into nine branches that flow into the great ocean:
first, the Wúbái River; second, the Quń River; third, the Bàng River; fourth, the Wū... [River].

5. Jiang (River). Five: Jiamei Jiang (Beautiful and Auspicious River). Six: Guanjian Jiang (Ditch River). Seven: Yuanjiang (Source River). Eight: Linjiang (Granary River). Nine: Tijiang (Elevated River).
The Preface praises Master Zhao’s four treatises as being beyond measure and number, like the ocean.
Possessing the nature of innate wisdom and a mind as upright as a tree, he stands out preeminent among all others, like the wood of the *yuzhang* (camphor) tree.
Furthermore, his cognitive consciousness was pure, luminous, and vast beyond all things; he entered into profound resonance with the principle of the Dharmakāya.
Not a single dharma nor a single person has ever surpassed Master Zhaoshan.
Those who know the Master are rare. Returning to the Master, I have selected these ten pieces. If one says they do not know him, then the Master is truly noble.
"Those who know the Master are rare"—this single sentence borrows from the seventh chapter of Laozi’s *Daodejing*, titled "My Words Are Very Easy to Know.
That chapter states: "My words are very easy to know; they are very easy to practice. (Emperor Xuanzong’s commentary).
It is said: "My words accord with principle and are thus easy to understand; the matters are simple and thus easy to practice. The Lord Lao further stated:
"None in the world can know them, none can practice them. The Imperial Commentary notes: "The world stagnates in words and does not awaken;
matters follow their course but lack concise restraint; therefore, none can know them, none can practice them. The Lord Lao further stated: "Words have a source; matters..."
There is the "Lord" (*jun*). The Commentary by Xuanzong states: "As for 'speech,' it resides in principle (*li*); when principle is attained, speech is forgotten;

therefore, speech takes non-speech as its essence. As for 'affairs,' they reside in achievement; when the achievement is completed, there is no presiding agent; therefore, affairs take non-action as their Lord."
The Lord Lao further said: "It is precisely because they lack knowledge that they do not know me. The Imperial Commentary notes:
"It is because worldly people lack the knowledge of realization that they do not understand my teaching of wordlessness and non-action."
The Lord Lao further said: "Those who know me are rare; therefore, those who conform to me are precious. Emperor Xuan’s commentary states:
"Those who fully understand the intent of my teaching on forgetting words are few and rare; the principle of my teaching on not speaking is supremely precious. The Lord Lao further said:
"Therefore, the sage wears coarse cloth while harboring jade within. Emperor Xuan’s commentary states: "Wearing coarse cloth means to remain hidden."

Externally, those who harbor kingship clarify its internal essence; thus, those who truly know it are rare. The Preface author altered the character "Lao" (Old) in the title of the Lord Lao to the character "Gong" (Duke).
At that time, people merely submitted to and followed the textual formulations of the Four Treatises. △ Third:
Rejoicing at the Fortunate Encounter.

I, Da, have attained the good fortune of being born in this world and encountered these sublime sounds. My joy and exultation are unceasing, and I never tire of partaking in this banquet of the Dharma.

Whenever I open and examine them, I cannot help but clap my hands and dance. I vow that throughout every lifetime until the end of my life, I shall propagate and expound them. My feelings toward the surviving writings of Sengzhao are just like this.
"Vainly born" (yōushō) means being born many times. "Heavenly fortune" (tenkō) refers to encountering [the truth] spontaneously without expectation.
"Correct sound" (shōon) refers to these four treatises; they are the authentic scriptural seals that accord with the Buddha-mind. "To partake" (kyō) means the time of eating.
"Feasting" refers to the time of sleep and rest. The "Preface Master" speaks for himself.

His statement that he has read the *Four Treatises* for many days without weariness, and that his hands move as if dancing, borrows from Zixia’s Preface to the *Odes*, which says, "I know not how my hands dance and my feet leap," expressing the height of joy.
When he says "the remaining texts of Sengzhao," he is referring to the *Four Treatises*; he simply vows never to abandon them lightly.
"How much more so for the *Madhyamaka-śāstra*, the *Śata-śāstra*, and the profound Vaipulya sūtras—would they not be free from increase?
The word "how much more so" (*kuàng*) indicates a comparison of similar categories. The Preface Master [Sengrui] refers here to Zhi’s four treatises;
when compared with the *Mādhyamika-śāstra*, the *Dharmaparyāya-prakāśamukha-śāstra*, and the extensive *Avataṃsaka* and other sūtras, there is not a single word added.
△ Fourth, the rejection of slanderous accusations:
The worldly rumors all say that because these were composed by Sengzhao, they must be sincere and represent the true truth; that the *Dilun* school is their ultimate source;
and that the teachings of Zhuangzi and Laozi are merely wild and reckless fabrications.

"Worldly rumors" are the unfounded talk of the mundane world. After Master Zhao’s passing, those who remained stubbornly attached to teachings concerning names and forms derided and slandered his *Four Treatises*.

Their writings were indeed based on the meaning of the *Ultimate Truth* (*paramārtha-satya*) from the *Tattvasiddhi-śāstra* and the meaning of the "Pervasive Principle" (*tongzong*) from the *Daśabhūmika-vibhāṣā-śāstra*, further embellished and supplemented by the terminology found in the texts of Zhuangzi and Laozi; they were thus wildly reckless.
As for this claim, it borrows a single phrase from the "Qi Wu" chapter of the *Zhuangzi*; it is a statement lacking fundamental basis or essential significance.
Furthermore, others have mocked and slandered it. Since there has already been such mockery and calumny in the past, such strife, jealousy, and malice are even more prevalent today.
For instance, during the Jiayou era, the Chan Master Mingjiao Qisong of Mount Dongshan in Tengzhou submitted [his work].

The *Zhengzong ji* (Record of the Orthodox Lineage) in twelve fascicles, compiled for Emperor Renzong, was subsequently ordered by imperial decree to be distributed to the Translation Institute (*Yijingyuan*).
It was then printed alongside the Tripitaka and disseminated throughout the realm; such gracious recognition and praise had never before been accorded to a work in antiquity.
At that time, the physician-monk Zifang possessed abundant robes and alms-bowls, and consequently, he convened those of shallow learning at the Suzhou Terrace (*Sutai*).
The practitioners of Chan and Vinaya composed written texts to slander the Chan school; furthermore, they commissioned their acquaintances in official positions to provide prefaces and publish them.
Throughout antiquity and the present, there have been no such heterodox practitioners as these.
These are truly the words of a great venomous insect (jugu), deceiving and defaming those who have passed away. The vulgar sounds of the streets and alleys are not worth so much as picking up.
"Great venomous insect" refers to words of great toxicity. Since the death of the Master, these poisonous and vulgar sounds have been used to deceive the sages and mislead the worthy;
they are certainly not worth listening to. Even during the Buddha’s lifetime, there were still five thousand who possessed overweening pride (*adhimāna*).
How much more so for those of today! △ Fifth, an exposition of the original intent:
Now, the Way of the Spirit has no fixed form, and the mind’s agility is difficult to depict. Since the written word is restrictive while the meaning is profound, the various perspectives diverge.
That the initial inquiry was not undertaken in vain is indeed for a good reason.
"The Way of the Divine has no form" means that the Dharma-body is without shape or image, like the great void.

"The mind is so subtle as to be difficult to depict" means that Prajñā is non-cognitive and likewise difficult to seek through signs or appearances. "Depicting" (huì) refers to copying, sketching, writing, or painting.

This refers to the Dharmakāya and the *prajñā* of contemplative illumination (*vipaśyanā*). It is quiescent yet ever-illuminating; illuminating yet ever-quiescent. It is free from all names and signs.
Regarding the phrase "the text is restrictive while the meaning is remote": within the four treatises, the wording is constrained and the principles are profound.
Therefore, Master Zhao had to rely on these foreign scriptures and their ornate phrasing as a means to enable later students to study *prajñā*.
It is easy for people to understand this; therefore, it is said that "it is where the various points diverge. "Various points" refers to the origins and sources of the four treatises.

"Where they diverge" means that Master Zhao has utilized the literary expressions of this land to translate and adapt the scriptures, which differ from the Sanskrit sounds of India. How could this be in vain?

"If one were to again follow and become intimate with their words, I pray that we may never meet face-to-face in any future birth until I attain the mind of patience (kṣānti-citta), at which point I shall return to deliver those who are inferior.
The Preface Master [Huiyuan] established these two dharmas to extensively protect the four treatises;

fearing that people of later generations would follow baseless rumors and slander them, he thus said, "If one were to again follow and become intimate with their words, I pray that we may never meet face-to-face in any future birth."
"Human beings meet one another. "To follow" (*xùn*) means to accord with; "to be familiar" (*xiá*) means to be intimate.

Aside from this, only when the master of the sequence has accomplished equal and perfect enlightenment and attained the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) can he then deliver and liberate those of such inferior faculties as these. △ Sixth:
Proclaiming the Meaning of the Preface.

I, Da, have frequented the lecture halls for over twenty years and have often encountered eminent scholars. Only recently did I come across this treatise, and I have composed this brief preface, entrusting my realization to its core.
May those who share my aspirations and those more virtuous than I await future sages to further elucidate it.

Before the Putong era of the Liang dynasty, when the Dharma had not yet reached this land, there were only formal lectures based on names and concepts; thus it is said, "lingering in the lecture halls.

Regarding the phrase "frequently encountering those who occupy the seat": *po* (頗) is glossed as "many. This means the author of the preface frequently met eminent masters who would challenge him for his seat.
As for "occupying the seat" (*chongxi* 重席): during every New Year’s audience in the Later Han dynasty, Emperor [Huan] would command the attendant *shizhong* Dai Ping to... [engage in debate].
When the Confucian scholars debated the classics, the victor would seize the seat; on that day, [Dai] prevailed by more than fifty rounds.
People of the time had a saying: "In debating the classics, none could exhaust Dai Shizhong.

Those who later encountered this treatise found that its author, though he had met many enlightened masters for over twenty years prior, finally encountered these four treatises at the end, each sentence of which was profound.
Having attained the principle of the Buddha, he differs from the aforementioned renowned masters; therefore, I have briefly composed this general preface.
It is my hope that it may manifest the depth of the Preface Master’s realization and his profound penetration of the meaning. Those who agree with me share the same realization as the Preface Master;
those who excel me possess a realization superior to that of the Preface Master. Both shall await future sages to judge their merits and demerits.
△ The Purpose of the Subsequent Introduction. There are four sections within this text: first, the sequence of the introduction; second, the elimination of characteristics; third, the eulogy;
and fourth, the distinction between what is this treatise and what is not. Now, the first is the sequence of the introduction.
As for the profound meaning of the "Great Division" (*mahābheda*), its designation is fundamentally non-existent.
The *Dvādaśamukha-śāstra* states: "The Great Division is emptiness (*śūnyatā*). It is not the emptiness of annihilation;
it is the principle of the true emptiness of the Dharma-body. Therefore, it is called the profound meaning."
Therefore, in establishing the fundamental purpose of this discourse, I have pointed toward the true mark (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).
The true mark is the absence of marks. This means that the essence of ultimate emptiness is fundamentally devoid of names and characteristics;
yet, within this absence of marks, one establishes [the teaching] without destroying conventional designations, thereby discoursing upon the true mark.
The path of the Dharma of emptiness cannot be surpassed by either the ultimate or the conventional; therefore, the two truths are explained next to reveal the gateway of the Buddha’s teaching.
Because true emptiness does not obstruct illusory existence, the function arises from the essence, whereby the myriad dharmas come to be. As the Teaching says:
The myriad phenomena of the universe and all things are sealed by a single Dharma; there is nothing that transcends the two truths of the ultimate and the conventional.
When the Snow Mountain Youth sought even half a verse, he sacrificed his body. A tree deity asked him, "What benefit does this verse provide?
The youth replied, "Such a verse is spoken by all Buddhas to open the path of the Dharma of emptiness; it is extracted from the *Nirvāṇa* [Sūtra]."
This is a sutra. The above constitutes the preface by the author, concerning the treatises *Wubiquan lun* (On the Non-transmigration of Things) and *Buzhenkong lun* (On the Non-emptiness of Reality).

Therefore, it says: "Next, the Two Truths are explained to manifest the gateway of the Buddha's teaching. This is because the gateway of the Buddha's teaching leads one out of the suffering of the triple world.
The teachings for a single lifetime do not transcend the two truths—the ultimate and the conventional—as their gateway.
However, as for the perfectly correct cause, it is none other than the unsurpassed *prajñā*; and as for the most ultimate fruit, it is only *nirvāṇa*.
Therefore, [the text] subsequently opens the double mystery to clarify that which is the abode of all sages.
The cause of perfect correctness is the primary cause of *nirvāṇa*. There is nothing superior to *prajñā*; this is the preface to the "Treatise on Namelessness.
That *prajñā* is non-cognition is the primary cause of *nirvāṇa*, and that *nirvāṇa* is nameless is the ultimate fruit of *prajñā*.
Therefore, I have prefixed this with the two treatises "On the Non-transmigration of Things" and "On the Non-emptiness of Reality," and followed it with [the discussion of] non-cognition and non-...
It is titled *The Two Treatises*. Thus it is said: "At the end, he opened up the double mystery. *Nirvāṇa* is one mystery; *Prajñā* is another mystery.

"At the end" refers to his later composition of these two treatises, *Wu zhi* (Non-knowing) and *Bu zhen kong* (Not Truly Empty), following his earlier works *Wu qian* (Non-migration) and *Bu zhen kong* (Not Truly Empty).
"Double mystery" borrows two phrases from the *Laozi Daodejing*: "Mystery upon mystery, the gate of all subtleties. Therefore...
It is said that "clarity" is the dwelling place of all sages. The preceding mention of the "True and the Conventional" refers to the first two treatises:

the non-transmigration of the conventional clarifies the True, and the non-true nature of the True clarifies the conventional. The subsequent mention of the "Twofold Mystery" refers to the latter two treatises;
both are the abodes of the Three Worthies and the Ten Sages. △ Second: Dispelling Characteristics.
Although its nature is likened to emptiness, there is no fundamental basis to be named. Its source transcends speech; it is not a realm where the mind operates.
When the mouth seeks to speak, words fail; when the mind seeks to contemplate, thought is lost. It cannot be known by wisdom, nor can it be cognized by consciousness.
This is not a state of lacking eloquence or lacking mind; rather, both verbal eloquence and mental discernment fall short of it. As for what the mind discriminates—
It is simply forgotten.
Thus, that which does not shift accords with the conventional; being conventional, it is non-arising.
This dispelling [of attachment] is precisely the illumination of the conventional as the ultimate.
The unreal is taken as real; "reality" is merely a verbal designation.
This negation clarifies reality by means of the conventional; it is spoken only in response to the capacities of sentient beings and possesses no actual substance—it serves to negate attachment.
If one can be vast and expansive, honoring this single path, it refers to the meaning of the fundamental source mentioned previously.

"Vast and expansive" means that one's own *dharmakāya* is like the great void—unobstructed and unimpeded—yet it does not reject the manifestation of various phenomena (*lakṣaṇa*), nor does it cling to the distinction between the ultimate and conventional truths or cause and effect. This is what is meant by "the single path."
The twelfth fascicle of the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states: "In the ground of the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), there is but a single path of purity; there is no other way.
To be pure of ear and empty of breast is the ineffable Two Truths."
"Purifying the ears" means that the nature of hearing is pure; it does not cling to the sounds of verbal teachings.

"Emptying the breast" means forgetting the self and severing discursive thought so as not to stagnate in empty stillness, nor to perceive the existence of the true or the conventional. This dispels the conceptual characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*) of the two aforementioned arguments.
Thus, the merit of pure illumination becomes manifest; therefore, while Prajñā is without cognition, the virtue of the Nameless arises, yet Nirvāṇa is not so designated.
If one does not cling to the causes and effects of the conventional and the ultimate, when the Prajñā of Contemplative Observation is absolutely realized by the person, [then] there is no cognition.
It is known that the function of skillful means is the manifestation of the "function of no-effort. To "manifest" is to be manifest.
This is precisely the Prajñā that is without cognition yet knows all things. It is precisely the Nirvāṇa that is nameless yet gives rise to wondrous functions.
△ Third: Praise.
I say that this exposition is comprehensive, exhausting the oceanic depths of the Buddha’s wisdom; it is vast and boundless, reaching the ultimate essence and characteristics of all phenomena.
The term "I" refers to the author of the preface himself. That this exposition is "comprehensive" points to the four treatises; "exhausting" means to have fully encompassed them.
There is not a single dharma that surpasses these four treatises; the nature and characteristics of awakening within them are vast and boundless, transcending all measure and number.

Although the words are concise, the meaning is rich; the phrasing is elegant, yet the principles reach their ultimate depth. The flow of the language is like an unbroken chain, while the underlying intent is truly solitary and expansive.

"Concise" means brief; "abundant" means complete. This refers to the fact that although the words in the Four Treatises are few, their principles are rich and comprehensive, encompassing the entire teaching of the Buddha throughout his lifetime.

"Elegant" refers to the fact that the phrasing and sentences within the Four Treatises are ornate, employing the scriptures and writings of this land as embellishments so that readers may understand them easily. Yet, every single sentence...
Reaching the realm of principle where all Buddhas dwell, the stream of discourse flows without interruption, like rings threaded upon a chain.
The meaning of this clarity regarding principle and phenomena stands solitary and peerless, transcending the limits of conceptual thought.
The phrase "linked rings" is derived from the thirty-second chapter of the *Zhuangzi*, "On All Under Heaven. This refers to the eloquence of Huizi; Huizi spoke of these "links."
The rings can be untied. This takes up the meaning of inexhaustibility. Guo Xiang’s commentary states: "As for the mutual threading of the rings, they are threaded through the empty space;
they are not threaded through the rings themselves. Therefore, the two rings thread through the space without intersecting one another, each turning independently.
Taking up the meaning of inexhaustibility, it can still be explained. The preface primarily refers to the discourse within the *Catuḥśataka* (Four Hundred Verses), although—
It is inexhaustible. Its profound resonance with the Buddha’s intent truly transcends the reach of words.
How could such exquisite and wonderful expressions fail to exhaustively present this grand discourse?
The Preface: Master Zhao’s *Four Treatises* (Sìlùn) excel both in literary style and doctrinal principle; this is borrowed from the words of Cáo Yōng regarding the Stele of Cáo É.
During the Han dynasty, Cáo Gǎn drowned while crossing the Zhèjiāng River. His daughter, Cáo É, aged fourteen, sought her father’s corpse but could not find it;
she threw herself into the Zhèjiāng and died. After one night had passed, she emerged holding her father’s corpse. Dú Shàng composed [the following] for her.
The Stele was situated on Mount Shangyu in Kuaiji. At the end of the Han dynasty, Cai Yong read it and inscribed eight characters upon its reverse side:
"Yellow silk, young woman, daughter's son, pickle mortar. Later, when Cao Cao was on military patrol with Yang Xiu, they came across these eight characters.
Cao Cao asked Xiu if he understood them; Xiu replied that he did. Cao Cao then ordered Xiu not to speak of it for the time being.
"Wait while I reflect upon it. After traveling thirty *li*, Cao finally understood. He then sighed to himself, saying, "Whether one has wisdom or lacks it makes a difference of thirty *li*.
Now, because of this military campaign, I have killed him. All of Cao's sons then entreated him to save [the man].
Cao Cao said, "Yang Xiu is a dragon among men; he is beyond the power of your control. He then had him executed. Shi Zhi explained:

"Yellow silk" (huáng juàn) refers to colored threads (sè sī), which is the character for "cutting" (jié). "Young lady" (yòu fù) refers to a young girl (shào nǚ), which is the character for "wondrous" (miào).
"Nephew's daughter" (wài sūn) refers to a woman (nǚ zǐ), which is the character for "excellent" (hǎo). "Pestle" (jī jiù) refers to that which receives pungency (shòu xīn).
"Shou-xin" (Receiving the Pungent) refers to the word "ci" (eloquence). The Preface Master praises the four treatises, noting that they are all of peerless and exquisite eloquence.
"Jie" means to exhaust or reach the limit; "hong" means great. The profound and subtle principles of the Buddha are entirely contained within these four great treatises.
This is why Kumārajīva sighed and said, "Master Zhaorong is the foremost among those who understand emptiness. These words were not without cause;

they are clearly recorded in the *Biographies of Eminent Monks* (Gaoseng zhuan) within the section on Huiguan. When Kumārajīva saw that Sengzhao had refined his prose and composed his writings, he leaned upon his desk and sighed, saying in brief: [...the rest of the passage...]

In truth, he was identical to Śubhūti; this has already been fully recounted in the preceding commentary. People of that time said that Master Kumārajīva had obtained Sengzhao, just as the Buddha had Śubhūti.
These words of praise are clearly manifest in the *Gaoseng zhuan* (Biographies of Eminent Monks).
"Han" refers to writing materials, such as bamboo slips or tablets. △ Fourth: Distinguishing what is this treatise and what is not.

However, the fundamental tenets are so transcendent that they cannot be subjected to critical interrogation. As for the four treatises beginning with *Buzhuan* (Non-Transmigration), they open the way to guide and attract [practitioners] through question-and-answer analysis of subtle points;
this is why they are called "treatises" (*lun*).
The phrase "the fundamental tenet is serene" (*zōngběn xiāorán*) refers to a state of serene vastness like empty space, whose boundaries and limits cannot be fathomed;
it is not the formal text of the treatise itself, but rather a general preface to the core principles of the four treatises.

Among these, the four—including *Wù bù qiān* ("All Things Do Not Shift")—use phenomena to clarify principles, providing instruction and guidance for beginners and those at the initial stage of their studies through a system of questions and answers that analyzes the principles with precision.
It is subtle; it investigates and scrutinizes the true from the false, which is why it is termed a "treatise" (lun).
